 Nebraska food insecurity reaches crisis point a year after SNAP changes 
 Advocates say 40,000 have lost benefits following work requirements and eligibility restrictions 
 A year after work requirements and eligibility restrictions took effect for SNAP, Nebraska advocates warn food insecurity is reaching a crisis point. By Macey Hansen Published : Oct. 22, 2026 at 7:46 AM CDT | Updated : 52 minutes ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google LINCOLN, Neb. (KOLN)—A year after H.R. 1, known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” led to new work requirements and eligibility restrictions for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program in Nebraska, advocates say food insecurity is nearing a crisis point. 
 Nebraska Appleseed hosted a virtual roundtable Tuesday with food banks and other organizations to discuss concerns over rising food insecurity across the state. The event brought together advocates working on food access and Nebraskans directly affected by the changes, who shared personal stories of struggle. 
 Joan Jakoubek, a Navy veteran and mother of two, said she relies on food pantries and housing through the VA but still struggles to afford groceries.
 “The reality is I’m still having to choose between food and rent,” Jakoubek said.
 Jakoubek said the new SNAP rules require veterans to work 80 hours a month in order to be eligible for food assistance. 
 “I knew I was going to fall short because I was only working 15 hours a week, as that’s all my employer had to give,” Jakoubek said.
 Requirements like the work-hour rule, including changes to exemptions for veterans and others, have caused issues for people trying to maintain benefits.
 Food banks working to fill gap 
 Charitable food organizations like the Food Bank of Lincoln are trying to help fill the gap for those facing these challenges.
 The Food Bank of Lincoln said it has seen a 45% increase in people served compared with five years ago. President and CEO Michaella Kumke says the Food Bank of Lincoln can meet current needs, but rising costs and increased demand are putting pressure on resources.
 “We are able to meet the need in this moment; it’s our concern that if the need continues at this rate,” Kumke said.
 According to a Nebraska Appleseed report, one in four SNAP participants—40,000 Nebraskans—have lost benefits since the changes took effect. Half of those who lost benefits are children. 
 Citing Feeding America’s Map of the Meal Gap, Kumke said Nebraska has a 15.8% food insecurity rate statewide, with Lancaster County over 15%. That is about 1 in 6 people facing food insecurity, meaning they have limited or uncertain access to adequate food. 
 Statewide concerns, DHHS response 
 In Omaha, Restoring Dignity serves refugee families who have also lost benefits because of the changes imposed a year ago. The organization said more than 2,300 people have come to them for help after losing food assistance, but it has had to turn people away.
 “We are denying families because we don’t have the resources to assist everyone,” said Hannah Vlach-Perez, executive director of Restoring Dignity. “And what we’re telling them is, ‘You got to go to food pantries.’”
 Vlach-Perez said some families are experiencing extreme hardships, adding:
 “Shame on our government for taking food away from children with cancer, shame on our government for making people with end-stage terminal illness have to suffer from malnutrition at the end of their lives, and shame on our government for hurting our local economies by erasing SNAP for thousands,” Vlach-Perez said.
 Advocates want officials to remove barriers for eligible people. They also said applicants have struggled to reach the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services for help with SNAP eligibility and the application process.
 The Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services said its processes are keeping error rates low. In a statement to 10/11, the agency said verification changes are required under federal rules to keep SNAP error rates below 6% and that it uses document verification to meet that requirement. A process that takes additional staff time. 
 “DHHS is aggressively recruiting and hiring staff, which will soon alleviate workloads and improve processing times, which will also reduce call volume and wait times,” the statement said.
